title: Alibri v. Detroit Wayne County Stadium Authority
lead: A landowner sells after being told her property is needed for stadium parking; the state supreme court reinstates relief based on an innocent but inaccurate representation.

actors.name: Freda Alibri
actors.role: Owner who conveyed property represented as necessary for stadium parking.

actors.name: Detroit Wayne County Stadium Authority
actors.role: Defendant whose inaccurate representation supplied the rescission ground.

proceedings: Wayne Circuit Court granted Alibri partial summary disposition and dismissed remaining claims on July 11, 2000.
After an adverse Court of Appeals decision, the Michigan Supreme Court reversed and reinstated that circuit-court order.
limits: Transactional details come from the assigned note; the complete reproduced Supreme Court order is short. No original reporter scan, individual authorship, vote division or monetary decree was recovered. The ruling does not decide the legality of threatened eminent domain.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A stadium project brings Alibri’s property into negotiations
sections.cue: What representation accompanied the requested sale?
paragraphs: The assigned account describes a downtown stadium project involving Detroit’s Downtown Development Authority, Wayne County, and the Detroit Lions and Tigers. Negotiations with property owner Freda Alibri began in 1996 because her land was represented as necessary for stadium parking. The authority threatened acquisition through eminent domain if needed.

According to that account, Alibri conveyed the property in January 1997 for $264,551.94. The stadium project and parking requirements were later downsized. The Michigan Supreme Court’s eventual order specifically identified the representation that all properties on the west side, including Alibri’s, were needed for project parking and the later determination that this was incorrect.

sections.title: The transaction reaches the state courts
sections.cue: Which earlier order did the Supreme Court ultimately restore?
paragraphs: Alibri’s litigation against the Detroit Wayne County Stadium Authority produced a July 11, 2000 Wayne Circuit Court order granting her partial summary disposition and dismissing the remaining claims. An intervening Court of Appeals decision displaced that result.

The Michigan Supreme Court granted leave to appeal and considered briefs and oral argument. It addressed whether the inaccurate representation about the need for the property justified rescission even though there was no indication that the defendant knew the statement was false.

sections.title: An innocent representation can support the identified rescission ground
sections.cue: Why was deliberate deceit unnecessary here?
paragraphs: The Supreme Court held that innocent misrepresentation justified rescission. The representation concerned an asserted need for Alibri’s property, and that assertion had been determined to be inaccurate. The order expressly noted that nothing indicated the defendant knew of the inaccuracy; the absence of demonstrated knowledge did not defeat this ground for relief.

The court cited United States Fidelity & Guaranty v. Black as authority concerning innocent misrepresentation. It did not base relief on intentional fraud or state that any later change in a development project automatically invalidates an earlier sale. Its short explanation addressed this representation and its established inaccuracy, without setting out a comprehensive elements test or a damages measure.

sections.title: The circuit-court order is reinstated on a somewhat different basis
sections.cue: What relief did the Supreme Court itself specify?
paragraphs: On July 20, 2004, the Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the specified circuit-court order, including dismissal of the remaining claims. Its innocent-misrepresentation ground differed somewhat from the circuit court’s basis.

The order did not calculate tort damages, prescribe the mechanics of reconveyance or repayment, or turn the assigned sale price into a new monetary decree. No separate writing or voting division is specified. The precise reported result is reinstatement of the earlier order, supported by rescission for the particular innocent misrepresentation.
